stem: The student wants to introduce the Saltmarsh Larval Census and its purpose to an audience unfamiliar with the program. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Saltmarsh Larval Census is a volunteer program based in Portugal.
• It was founded in 2009 by marine biologist Inês Carvalho.
• Volunteers set fine-mesh plankton nets at dusk in coastal estuaries.
• The program counts the larvae of crabs and other crustaceans to track how estuary populations change from year to year.
• In 2017, the program launched an offshoot, the Larval Atlas, an online map of its data.
choices: The Larval Atlas, an online map launched in 2017, displays the data that Saltmarsh Larval Census volunteers gather in coastal estuaries each year.
Founded in 2009 by marine biologist Inês Carvalho, the Saltmarsh Larval Census is a volunteer program whose members set plankton nets at dusk.
The Saltmarsh Larval Census, a volunteer program in Portugal, counts crab and other crustacean larvae to track how estuary populations change over time.
Since 2009, the Saltmarsh Larval Census has recorded yearly shifts in estuary crustacean populations, data now mapped on the Larval Atlas.
explanation: The goal has two parts: introduce the program to readers who have never heard of it, and give its purpose. Choice C does both in one sentence. The appositive 'a volunteer program in Portugal' tells a newcomer what the Census is, and 'to track how estuary populations change over time' states what it is for. It leaves out the founder, the method and the offshoot, because the goal doesn't need them.

A.why: You saw a name followed by an identifying appositive and stopped checking. But the label belongs to the Larval Atlas, the offshoot, not to the Census. The Census is mentioned only in passing, as if the reader already knows it, and its purpose never appears.

B.why: This choice survives the first test: it tells you the Census is a volunteer program. But the goal also asks for its purpose, and this sentence gives only the founding details and the method (setting nets at dusk). It never says why the volunteers count larvae. You checked 'introduce' and forgot 'and its purpose.'

D.why: This one comes close to the purpose, since it mentions recording shifts in populations. But it never says what the Census is, so it treats the program as already familiar. It also names a second unfamiliar thing, the Larval Atlas, without explaining it. That might work for an informed reader, but it fails the stated audience.

stem: The student wants to introduce the Halvorsen Shuttle Protocol to an audience unfamiliar with it, explaining what the protocol measures. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Halvorsen Shuttle Protocol is a fitness test.
• It was designed in 1994 by Norwegian exercise physiologist Erik Halvorsen.
• Athletes sprint repeatedly between two lines 20 meters apart, with rest intervals that shrink each round.
• It measures how quickly an athlete recovers between bursts of high-intensity effort.
• In 2011, a shorter version, the Mini-Halvorsen, was created for youth soccer academies.
choices: Norwegian exercise physiologist Erik Halvorsen designed the Halvorsen Shuttle Protocol in 1994, in which athletes sprint between lines 20 meters apart.
The Halvorsen Shuttle Protocol, a fitness test of repeated 20-meter sprints, measures how quickly an athlete recovers between bursts of intense effort.
The Mini-Halvorsen, a shorter fitness test created in 2011 for youth soccer academies, adapts the longer Halvorsen Shuttle Protocol.
Because its rest intervals shrink each round, the Halvorsen Shuttle Protocol reveals how quickly an athlete recovers between bursts of intense effort.
explanation: A reader who has never heard of the protocol first needs to know what it is, and the goal also asks what it measures. Choice B covers both. The appositive 'a fitness test of repeated 20-meter sprints' identifies the protocol as a type of thing, and the main clause states what it measures: recovery between bursts of high-intensity effort.

A.why: You looked for an identifying label and found one, but it's attached to the wrong noun. 'Norwegian exercise physiologist' tells you who Erik Halvorsen is, not what his protocol is. The sentence describes the sprints but never says what the protocol measures, which is the specific thing the goal asks for.

C.why: This is the subtype's trap. It gives a clear label, but to the Mini-Halvorsen, a later offshoot. It mentions the main protocol only as something already known and never says what either test measures.

D.why: This is the trap that survives the first insight. It does state what the protocol measures, so it seems to meet the goal. But it never says the protocol is a fitness test, and 'its rest intervals' and 'each round' refer to a structure the reader hasn't been told about. The sentence assumes the reader already knows what the protocol is, so it fails the stated audience.

stem: The student wants to introduce ikat to an audience unfamiliar with textile techniques, making clear what distinguishes it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Ikat is a technique for dyeing yarn.
• In ikat, bundles of yarn are tightly bound and then dyed before they are woven.
• As a result, the cloth's pattern exists in the threads before the cloth itself does.
• The name comes from the Malay word mengikat, "to tie."
• Ikat is practiced in Indonesia, Uzbekistan, Guatemala, and elsewhere.
• Double ikat, in which both sets of threads are bound and dyed, is made in only a few places, including Patan, India.
choices: Ikat, a dyeing technique practiced from Indonesia to Guatemala, takes its name from the Malay word mengikat, which means "to tie."
In ikat, a dyeing technique, yarn is bound and dyed before weaving, so the pattern exists in the threads before the cloth does.
Double ikat, in which both sets of threads are bound and dyed before weaving, is made today in only a few places, such as Patan, India.
Ikat's tightly bound bundles of yarn, tied as its Malay root suggests, are dyed in places as far apart as Uzbekistan and Guatemala.
explanation: The goal asks for two things: tell a newcomer what ikat is, and say what sets it apart. Choice B labels ikat as a dyeing technique, then gives the defining feature: the yarn is dyed before it is woven, so the pattern exists before the cloth does. Choice A also gives a label, but the 'distinguishing' part stops at where the word comes from.

A.why: You saw the label 'a dyeing technique' and stopped checking. Plenty of dyeing techniques exist. A word's origin and a list of places that use it don't tell a newcomer what makes ikat different.

C.why: This is the subtype's trap. It describes a variant, double ikat, and treats ikat itself as something you already know. A reader who has never heard of ikat learns nothing about the basic technique.

D.why: This mentions bound yarn but never says ikat is a dyeing technique or that the dyeing happens before weaving. It assumes the reader already knows what 'ikat's bundles' means.

stem: The student wants to introduce Glossopteris to an audience unfamiliar with it and explain why its fossils interest geologists. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Glossopteris is an extinct genus of seed ferns.
• Its name comes from the Greek glossa, "tongue," for its long, tapering leaves.
• Fossils of Glossopteris have been found in South America, Africa, India, Antarctica, and Australia.
• These landmasses are now separated by oceans.
• In the early twentieth century, the plant's distribution was cited as evidence that these landmasses were once joined.
choices: Named for the Greek word for "tongue," Glossopteris was an extinct genus of seed ferns whose leaves were long and tapering.
Fossils of Glossopteris, found on five landmasses now separated by oceans, were cited as evidence that the landmasses were once joined.
Glossopteris, an extinct seed fern, left fossils on five landmasses now separated by oceans, which suggested they had once been joined.
Glossopteris fossils have turned up in South America, Africa, India, Antarctica, and Australia, five landmasses separated by oceans today.
explanation: Two conditions have to hold together: say what Glossopteris is, and say why its fossils matter. Choice C labels it as an extinct seed fern and connects where its fossils are found to the idea that those continents were once joined. B gives the significance, but a newcomer never learns whether Glossopteris is a plant, an animal, or a rock.

A.why: This handles the introduction well, with a label and the name's origin, but it drops the second half of the goal. Nothing here says why geologists care.

B.why: This is the second-order trap. Once you've spotted the geological point, this choice looks complete. But it never says what Glossopteris is, so it treats the name as already familiar, which fails the stated audience.

D.why: This lists the locations but neither labels Glossopteris nor draws the conclusion that the landmasses were once joined. Where something was found isn't the same as why that matters.

stem: The student wants to introduce Silbo Gomero to an audience unfamiliar with it, making clear how it relates to Spanish. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Silbo Gomero is used on La Gomera, one of Spain's Canary Islands.
• It is not a separate language; it is a way of transmitting Spanish by whistling.
• Whistlers replace spoken vowels and consonants with changes in pitch.
• A whistled message can carry several kilometers across the island's deep ravines.
• Silbo Gomero has been taught in La Gomera's schools since 1999.
• UNESCO recognized it as cultural heritage in 2009.
choices: Silbo Gomero, a way of whistling Spanish used on the Canary Island of La Gomera, replaces spoken sounds with changes in pitch.
Silbo Gomero, a whistled language of the Canary Islands, can carry a message several kilometers across La Gomera's deep ravines.
Because it is whistled rather than spoken, Silbo Gomero carries several kilometers, which suits the deep ravines of La Gomera.
Taught in La Gomera's schools since 1999, Silbo Gomero was recognized by UNESCO as part of the world's cultural heritage in 2009.
explanation: The goal requires a label that correctly places Silbo Gomero in relation to Spanish. Choice A calls it 'a way of whistling Spanish' and adds how it works, so a newcomer knows what it is and how it connects to the spoken language.

B.why: This copies the right form, an appositive label after the name, but the label is wrong. The notes say outright that Silbo Gomero is not a separate language, and calling it 'a whistled language' gets wrong exactly the relationship the goal asks you to explain.

C.why: This explains why whistling is practical but never mentions Spanish, so it doesn't do the job the goal names.

D.why: This is the subtype's trap. It leans on dates and recognition and treats Silbo Gomero as already known, so a reader who has never heard of it still doesn't know what it is.

stem: The student wants to introduce the kakapo to an audience unfamiliar with it, emphasizing what sets it apart from other parrots. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The kakapo is a parrot found only in New Zealand.
• It is the only parrot species that cannot fly.
• Adults can weigh up to 4 kilograms, making it the heaviest parrot in the world.
• Kakapo are active at night.
• They breed only in years when rimu trees produce heavy crops of fruit.
• A recovery program has monitored the species since 1995 and has named every living bird.
choices: A flightless, nocturnal bird of New Zealand, the kakapo breeds only in years when rimu trees produce heavy crops of fruit.
Every living kakapo has been named by the recovery program that has monitored the species in New Zealand since 1995.
Kakapo are active at night and breed only in years when New Zealand's rimu trees produce especially heavy crops of fruit.
The kakapo, a New Zealand parrot, is the only parrot that cannot fly and, at up to 4 kilograms, the heaviest parrot as well.
explanation: The goal sets the comparison: the kakapo against other parrots. Choice D tells a newcomer it is a parrot and gives two features no other parrot shares, flightlessness and weight.

A.why: This is the second-order trap. It has an identifying label and even mentions flightlessness, so it looks like an introduction. But 'bird' is the wrong category for the goal. A reader never learns the kakapo is a parrot, so 'flightless' isn't framed as unusual among parrots, and the rest goes to a breeding detail.

B.why: This is the subtype's trap. It focuses on the recovery program and assumes the reader already knows what a kakapo is.

C.why: This gives behaviour but no label and no contrast with other parrots, so it treats the kakapo as already familiar.

stem: The student wants to introduce directly observed therapy to an audience unfamiliar with it, explaining its purpose. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Directly observed therapy (DOT) is a method of delivering medication.
• In DOT, a health worker watches a patient take each dose.
• It is widely used for tuberculosis, whose treatment lasts at least six months.
• Its aim is to prevent missed doses, which can allow drug-resistant bacteria to develop.
• Video-observed therapy, a newer variant, lets the health worker watch over a smartphone.
choices: Directly observed therapy, often used for tuberculosis, is a method in which a health worker watches a patient take each dose.
In directly observed therapy, a health worker watches a patient take each dose to prevent the missed doses that breed drug resistance.
Video-observed therapy, a newer variant of DOT, lets a health worker watch a patient take each dose over a smartphone.
To prevent the missed doses that breed drug resistance during tuberculosis treatment, many health programs rely on DOT.
explanation: The goal needs both what DOT is and why it's done. Choice B explains the method (a health worker watches each dose) and gives its purpose (preventing missed doses that lead to drug resistance), using the full name so a newcomer can follow.

A.why: This is a good introduction to the method, with a label and a description, but it never gives the purpose. The goal says 'explaining its purpose,' and this stops before that.

C.why: This is the subtype's trap. It introduces an offshoot and uses the abbreviation 'DOT' as if the reader already knows the original method.

D.why: This is the second-order trap. It gives the purpose, but it names the method only by an unexplained abbreviation and never says what DOT involves, which fails an unfamiliar audience.

stem: The student wants to introduce the Dymaxion map to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Buckminster Fuller was an American architect and inventor.
• In 1943, Life magazine published his Dymaxion map.
• The Dymaxion map is a world map made by projecting the globe onto a twenty-sided solid and unfolding it flat.
• It shows the continents with little distortion in their relative sizes.
• Unlike the Mercator projection, it does not enlarge landmasses near the poles.
• It has no fixed top or bottom.
choices: Buckminster Fuller, an American architect and inventor, published his Dymaxion map in a 1943 issue of Life magazine.
Unlike the Mercator projection, the Dymaxion map does not enlarge the landmasses that lie close to the North and South Poles.
The Dymaxion map, a world map made by unfolding a twenty-sided solid flat, shows the continents with little distortion in size.
Having no fixed top or bottom, the Dymaxion map can be turned in any direction without being considered upside down.
explanation: A newcomer first needs to know what the Dymaxion map is. Choice C attaches the label 'a world map' to the name, explains how it's made, and says what it accomplishes.

A.why: This is the second-order trap. It uses the appositive-label pattern you were taught to look for, but the label describes Fuller, not the map. A reader learns who made the Dymaxion map and when, but not what it is.

B.why: This turns into a comparison and assumes the reader knows both the Dymaxion map and the Mercator projection. It never says what the Dymaxion map is.

D.why: This is the subtype's trap. It picks out one secondary feature and treats the map as already known, without saying it's a world map or how it's made.

stem: The student wants to introduce the glycemic index to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The glycemic index (GI) is a scale from 0 to 100.
• It ranks carbohydrate foods by how quickly they raise blood sugar, compared with pure glucose, which is set at 100.
• It was developed in 1981 by David Jenkins, a researcher at the University of Toronto.
• Glycemic load, a later measure, also accounts for portion size.
• Watermelon has a high GI but a low glycemic load.
choices: The glycemic index, a scale developed in 1981 at the University of Toronto, assigns pure glucose a value of 100.
Glycemic load, a measure developed after the glycemic index, also takes into account the size of a food portion.
Watermelon has a high glycemic index but a low glycemic load, because a typical serving contains little carbohydrate.
The glycemic index, a 0-to-100 scale, ranks carbohydrate foods by how quickly they raise blood sugar compared with glucose.
explanation: A newcomer needs to know what the glycemic index is and what it measures. Choice D labels it as a 0-to-100 scale and says what it ranks and against what benchmark.

A.why: This is the second-order trap. It gives the label 'a scale,' so it passes the first check, but it never says what the scale measures. Knowing that glucose scores 100 means nothing if you don't know what the score is for.

B.why: This is the subtype's trap. It introduces a later offshoot measure and treats the glycemic index as already familiar.

C.why: This uses an example that assumes the reader knows both terms, and its explanation (that a typical serving contains little carbohydrate) isn't in the notes.

stem: The student wants to introduce the Aarne-Thompson-Uther index to an audience unfamiliar with it, explaining what scholars use it for. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Aarne-Thompson-Uther (ATU) index is a catalog of folktale types.
• It assigns each tale type a number; Cinderella stories, for example, are type 510A.
• It lets scholars compare versions of the same story told in different cultures.
• Finnish folklorist Antti Aarne published the first version in 1910.
• It was expanded by Stith Thompson and most recently revised by Hans-Jörg Uther in 2004.
choices: The Aarne-Thompson-Uther index, a numbered catalog of folktale types, lets scholars compare versions of one story told in different cultures.
Finnish folklorist Antti Aarne published the first version of the index in 1910, and Hans-Jörg Uther revised it most recently in 2004.
In the ATU index, stories of the Cinderella type are numbered 510A, a label that scholars use for versions from many different cultures.
The Aarne-Thompson-Uther index, a catalog of folktale types first compiled in 1910, was revised most recently by Hans-Jörg Uther in 2004.
explanation: The goal combines an introduction with a use. Choice A labels the index as a numbered catalog of folktale types and says what scholars do with it: compare versions of one story across cultures.

B.why: This is the subtype's trap. It's built on people and dates, and the only label belongs to Aarne, not the index, so a newcomer never learns what the index is.

C.why: This uses an unexplained abbreviation and starts with a specific entry, treating the index as already known. It hints at a use but never says the index is a catalog.

D.why: This is the second-order trap. It gets the introduction right with a correct label, then spends the rest on dates and never explains what scholars use the index for, which is the second half of the goal.
